newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Guatemala, China agree on UN peacekeepers.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala, China agree on UN peacekeepers.

text.p: China and Guatemala on Monday reached an agreement on rescuing a U.N. peacekeeping mission that China had vetoed in the Security Council because of Guatemala's ties to Taiwan, the United Nations announced.
"Agreement was reached that will permit the Security Council to return to the issue," U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said, adding that a formal council meeting was expected later in the day.
Details were vague on the terms of the solution, but the council was expected to approve 155 military observers for three months to monitor Guatemala's peace accords.
Beijing did not object to the peacekeeping mission itself but was reacting to Guatemala's diplomatic and other ties with Taiwan, regarded by China as a renegade province.

Chinese and Guatemalan representatives were meeting with the so-called friends of Guatemala -- the United States, Mexico, Colombia, Norway, Venezuela and Spain -- at Mexico's U.N. mission to work out final details of the understanding.

One element was said to be an undertaking by Guatemala to refrain in future from co-sponsoring an annual General Assembly resolution aimed at securing U.N. membership for Taiwan, which was expelled from the world body in 1971 and replaced by Beijing as the rightful representative of China.

On Jan. 10, the 14 other Security Council members all supported sending the peacekeepers to Guatemala for a three-month period. But a negative vote by China, one of five permanent council members with veto power, killed the mission.

Last week two leaders of the rebel Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) came to New York to lobby China in favor of the U.N.-brokered peace accords, signed on Dec. 29, that ended three decades of civil war. Under those agreements, the army is to cut its numbers and the guerrillas are to go to assembly points, disarm and be integrated into civilian life.

Diplomats said China was not asking for a break in diplomatic relations between Guatemala and Taiwan as a condition for supporting the peacekeepers. But among its demands were that Guatemala stop supporting moves to put U.N. membership for Taiwan on the General Assembly's agenda.

For the past four years Guatemala has been among a number of small countries, mainly from Central America, the Caribbean and Africa, which have sought the inscription of a new General Assembly agenda item aimed at establishing a committee to consider U.N. membership for Taiwan. The move has been blocked each time in the assembly's steering committee.

Another Chinese demand, the diplomats said, was a public apology from Guatemala for inviting Taiwan's foreign minister, John Chang, to the Dec. 29 peace signing ceremonies. But Guatemala has refused to do this.
